# Diagnosing a Post-Overheat Startup Failure on a 2007 Nissan Murano

When an engine overheats and subsequently shuts down, the immediate reaction is often to assume the battery or fuel system is at fault once the vehicle won't start. You have already addressed the low-hanging fruit: a new battery, replaced fuses, fresh spark plugs, and coils. The fact that the engine cranks but fails to fire, accompanied by a sound resembling running out of gas, combined with water exiting the exhaust, points to a specific failure mode common in this generation of V6 engines.

The critical observation here is the water in the exhaust pipe. In a normally operating internal combustion engine, combustion gases exit through the tailpipe. If you are seeing liquid water, that indicates the cylinder head gasket has likely failed catastrophically or a cracked cylinder head is allowing coolant to enter the combustion chamber. This condition often precipitates when an engine overheats; excessive heat warps the metal surfaces, breaking the seal between the coolant passages and the cylinders.

The auditory cue you are hearingâresembling running out of gasâis actually the sound of raw fuel being injected into a cylinder that is trying to compress liquid rather than air-fuel vapor. When the pistons move down during the intake stroke, they are pulling in gasoline instead of an oxygenated charge because the coolant has flooded the combustion space. This creates an extremely rich mixture that cannot ignite properly, even with fresh spark plugs and functional coils. The fuel pump may be draining power (as you noted), but the fuel is being wasted into a compromised chamber rather than contributing to combustion.

This scenario presents a dangerous trade-off for anyone attempting to jump-start or crank the engine further. Attempting to start the vehicle under these conditions forces unburnt, super-heated coolant through the exhaust valve train and can rapidly clog the catalytic converter with molten aluminum and silicon deposits from the block. Once a converter is damaged by this process, it becomes a restrictive back-pressure nightmare, often leading to complete engine failure or a fire hazard if the undercarriage gets hot enough to ignite leaking fuel lines.

Before proceeding with any further diagnostics or repair attempts, you must confirm the source of the coolant intrusion. The most reliable method is a compression test or a leak-down test performed after the engine has cooled completely. If compression is low on one cylinder while others are normal, or if you see bubbles rising in the coolant reservoir when the engine is running (with the radiator cap off), the diagnosis is confirmed: the mechanical seal is broken.

There is no amount of fuel system cleaning or wiring harness inspection that will resolve a physical breach between the cooling and combustion systems. The "running out of gas" sensation is a symptom of the wrong fluid being in the wrong place, not an actual lack of fuel. Given the age of the vehicle (2007 model year) and the specific failure mode triggered by overheating, the cost-benefit analysis often favors addressing the root mechanical failure immediately rather than continuing to drain the battery and risk further collateral damage to the catalytic converter or transmission cooler lines, which are integral to this V6's operation.
